What did we develop? A website that serves as a quantitative planetary-analogy simulator, together with a matrix that links lunar sites (Apollo 11, 15 and 17) and Martian sites (Syrtis Major, Nirgal Vallis, Viking 1 and Schiaparelli) to five terrestrial environments: Devon Island, Utah, Askja, Atacama and the McMurdo Dry Valleys. The simulator scores each Earth site from 0 to 10 across eight weighted dimensions and calculates weighted similarity, cosine similarity and logistic suitability probability.
How does it address the challenge? It turns qualitative comparison into a reproducible, adjustable ranking (editable weights, threshold and sensitivity). In the test with Viking 1 (Chryse Planitia), McMurdo ranked first with 88% similarity and a 96.9% suitability probability; it was followed by Devon Island, Askja and Atacama, while Utah fell below the 65% threshold.
Why is it important? No Earth site fully replicates another world; knowing which one serves which aspect makes it possible to test rovers, drills, suits and operations more precisely, more economically and more safely before establishing permanent bases on the Moon and Mars.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Analog Finders is a quantitative planetary-analogy simulator with a companion website. It compares lunar sites (Apollo 11, 15 and 17) and Martian sites (Syrtis Major, Nirgal Vallis, Viking 1 and Schiaparelli) with five Earth environments: Devon Island, Utah, Askja, Atacama and the McMurdo Dry Valleys. The user chooses a target site and sets the weights of eight dimensions (geology, terrain, temperature, water/ice, dust and wind, biology, caves/subsurface, and operations). Each Earth site is scored from 0 to 10 in every dimension, using NASA open data (MOLA, THEMIS and SHARAD for Mars; LOLA, LROC, Diviner and Mini-RF for the Moon). The Excel simulator then calculates weighted similarity, cosine similarity and a logistic suitability probability (threshold X0 = 0.65, sensitivity k = 15) and ranks the sites. In our test with Viking 1 (Chryse Planitia), the McMurdo Dry Valleys ranked first with 88% similarity and 96.9% suitability probability, while Utah fell below the threshold.

What benefits does it offer?

It turns a qualitative comparison into a reproducible, adjustable ranking that other teams can repeat, since weights, threshold and sensitivity are editable. It shows which Earth site is best for which purpose, so rovers, drills, suits and operations can be tested more precisely, more economically and more safely before real missions. It is transparent about limits, because it reports separately the dimensions where a site falls below the threshold. It is also accessible: it relies on open NASA data and an Excel spreadsheet, so it can be used and verified without advanced programming.

What is the expected impact of the project?

The project gives space agencies, researchers and new teams an orderly way to decide where to train and test technology before establishing permanent bases on the Moon and Mars. By identifying where an analogy is strong and where it stops being valid (gravity, atmosphere, radiation and biology), it supports better mission preparation at lower cost and risk. The model is scalable: it can be applied to other lunar and Martian sites and to new Earth candidates, even ones not yet studied as analogs, simply by scoring the eight dimensions.

What tools, programming languages, hardware or software did you use to develop your project?

Data and platforms: NASA open data (MOLA, THEMIS, SHARAD, LOLA, LROC, Diviner, Mini-RF), accessed through NASA Mars Trek and JMARS, plus the open resources of NASA Space Apps. Programming: Python, to obtain and process the data. Software: Microsoft Excel for the simulator (weighted similarity, cosine similarity and logistic probability), and HTML for the project website, published on Netlify. Artificial intelligence: Claude (by Anthropic) helped generate and run the Python code, build the Excel simulator and the HTML code, and add images and animations; the team reviewed all results. Documents: a comparative matrix of planetary analogy (Mars, Moon, Earth) and a cross-correspondence matrix, used as the documentary basis for the scores.

In what way is your project creative?

Instead of describing analog sites one by one, we built a single multi-criteria method that links the Moon, Mars and Earth. It combines three complementary metrics (weighted similarity, cosine similarity and logistic probability) in an Excel tool anyone can edit. A cross-correspondence matrix groups sites into four types of analog environments (basaltic plains and cold regolith; canyons, strata and contacts; hyperarid plains and buried ice; impact basins, paleolakes and salts). The team, new to hackathons and with limited programming experience, used AI as a collaborator to turn open data into a working simulator and website.

What factors did your team take into account?

We considered eight dimensions that matter for exploration: geology and materials, terrain and topography, temperature and illumination, water and ice (ISRU resources), dust, wind and erosion, biology and habitability, caves and subsurface, and operations and landing. We also weighed the limits of any analogy (gravity, atmosphere, radiation and biology), the mission purpose when assigning weights, and the use of open, verifiable data. We were also mindful of our own limitations: scores and weights are team-assigned criteria that should be backed by measured values and a sensitivity analysis, only one target site has been simulated so far, the sample is small (5 Earth sites), and the null hypothesis has not yet been statistically tested.
